overview.title: Local patterns: translation invariance and spatial hierarchies
overview.main_topic: Why learning local patterns in small windows gives ConvNets two key properties: translation-invariant patterns and spatial hierarchies of patterns.
overview.central_idea: Convolution layers learn patterns in small 2D windows (3 × 3 in the MNIST model). Because the same pattern detector is applied everywhere, a pattern learned at one location is recognized at any location (data efficiency), and stacking layers composes small patterns into larger, more abstract ones, mirroring a visual world that is translation invariant and spatially hierarchical.
overview.importance: This page answers the question posed on p.258 (why the ConvNet beats the dense model) at the conceptual level. These two properties are the main justification for using ConvNets on images throughout the rest of the book.
learning_objectives: Contrast global patterns (Dense) with local patterns (convolution) in small 2D windows.
Explain translation invariance and why it makes ConvNets data efficient.
Explain how stacked convolution layers learn a spatial hierarchy of patterns.
Read figure 8.1 (local patches of a digit) and figure 8.2 (edges -> parts -> 'cat').
prerequisites: The MNIST ConvNet with 3 × 3 Conv2D layers (p.256-258)
Dense layers and what their weights connect to
The idea of generalization and sample efficiency

summary:
Continuing the sentence begun on p.258, the authors state the fundamental difference between layer types: `Dense` layers learn **global** patterns (for an MNIST digit, patterns involving all pixels), whereas convolution layers learn **local** patterns, i.e. patterns found in small 2D windows of the input. In the MNIST ConvNet these windows were all 3 × 3. Figure 8.1 shows a handwritten digit with several small square windows highlighted; each extracted patch contains a simple local pattern such as a stroke fragment or edge.

This local character gives ConvNets two properties:

1. **The patterns they learn are translation invariant.** After learning a pattern in the lower-right corner of an image, a ConvNet can recognize it anywhere, e.g. in the upper-left corner. A densely connected model would have to learn the pattern anew at every new location. Hence ConvNets are **data efficient** on images, because *the visual world is fundamentally translation invariant*: they need fewer training samples to learn representations that generalize.
2. **They can learn spatial hierarchies of patterns.** A first convolution layer learns small local patterns such as edges; a second learns larger patterns made of first-layer features; and so on. This lets ConvNets efficiently learn increasingly complex and abstract visual concepts, because *the visual world is fundamentally spatially hierarchical*.

Figure 8.2 illustrates the hierarchy: a cat image at the bottom is decomposed into elementary lines and textures (a row of small boxes with curves and strokes), which combine into simple object parts (an eye, a nose, an ear), which in turn combine into the high-level concept "cat" at the top.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Completing the sentence from p.258: Dense layers learn patterns involving all pixels, whereas convolution layers learn local patterns in small 2D windows (3 × 3 in the previous example). This gives ConvNets two interesting properties.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A Dense unit's weights span the full 784-pixel image, so the 'pattern' it learns is a whole-image template. A convolution filter has weights only for a 3 × 3 neighbourhood (times the input channels), and is evaluated at each location. Figure 8.1 makes this concrete: a digit can be described by a handful of small patches, each containing a simple edge or stroke.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Locality is the architectural prior that the next two bullets derive consequences from.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Restricting each output to a small receptive field and sharing the same weights across positions: these two constraints define convolution.

terminology.meaning: A pattern contained in a small window of the input, like a 3 × 3 patch.
The small region (patch) of the input a convolution filter looks at at one time.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Patterns learned by a ConvNet are translation invariant: a pattern learned in the lower-right corner can be recognized anywhere, e.g. in the upper-left. A dense model would have to relearn it at each new location. This makes ConvNets data efficient on images, because the visual world is fundamentally translation invariant; they need fewer training samples to learn representations that generalize.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Because a single filter is applied at every position, a detector trained on examples where a stroke appears in one corner automatically works in every other corner. A Dense layer has separate weights per pixel, so 'diagonal stroke at top-left' and 'diagonal stroke at bottom-right' are unrelated to it; it needs training examples of both. Since images contain the same objects at all sorts of positions, building this in saves many training examples.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Data efficiency is the practical reason ConvNets can be trained from scratch on small image datasets (section 8.2) and why they beat the dense model on MNIST.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Strictly, the convolution operation is translation *equivariant* (shifting the input shifts the response map); combined with pooling and a final global pooling, the model's output becomes approximately invariant to translation. (Beyond the book.)

terminology.meaning: Recognizing a pattern regardless of where it appears in the image.
Needing fewer training samples to reach a given level of generalization.

connections: p.626: the conclusions restate that applying the same transformation to different patches yields translation-invariant, data-efficient representations.

paragraphs.what_it_says: ConvNets can learn spatial hierarchies: a first conv layer learns small local patterns such as edges, a second learns larger patterns made of first-layer features, and so on. This allows them to efficiently learn increasingly complex and abstract visual concepts, because the visual world is fundamentally spatially hierarchical.
paragraphs.what_it_means: Each layer's inputs are the previous layer's feature maps. A 3 × 3 window at layer 2 covers 3 × 3 positions of edge detectors, so it can detect combinations of edges (corners, curves); after pooling, each position covers more of the original image, so deeper layers see larger and more abstract structures. Figure 8.2 draws this as edges -> eye/nose/ear -> 'cat'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Hierarchy is how a network made of tiny 3 × 3 filters can ultimately recognize whole objects; it is also the basis for why lower layers transfer well across tasks (section 8.3).
paragraphs.technical_idea: Receptive field growth: with 3 × 3 kernels and 2 × 2 pooling, the effective region of the input seen by a unit grows layer by layer.

terminology.meaning: Organization of patterns where larger patterns are composed of smaller ones arranged in space.
A high-level notion such as 'cat' or 'eye', as opposed to raw edges.

concepts.name: Convolution (local pattern learning)
concepts.definition: A layer that learns local patterns in small 2D windows of its input and applies the same detector at every location.
concepts.intuition: Slide a small stamp over the picture and record how well each spot matches.
concepts.technical: Each output value depends only on a k × k window (3 × 3 here) of the input across all channels; weights are shared across positions.
concepts.significance: Gives ConvNets translation invariance and spatial hierarchies.
concepts.example: A 3 × 3 diagonal-stroke detector fires wherever a diagonal stroke appears in a digit.
concepts.misconception: Local does not mean the network only sees small regions: stacking layers lets deep units see large parts of the image.

concepts.name: Translation invariance
concepts.definition: The property that a pattern learned at one location is recognized at any location in the image.
concepts.intuition: An eye is an eye whether it is at the top or bottom of the photo.
concepts.technical: Follows from weight sharing: the same filter is evaluated at every position. Strictly the conv operation is translation-equivariant; pooling and global pooling make the final output (approximately) invariant. (The equivariance nuance is beyond the book.)
concepts.significance: Makes ConvNets data efficient: they need fewer samples to generalize, since a pattern need not be learned separately at each location.
concepts.example: Learned in the lower-right corner, recognized in the upper-left corner (the book's example).
concepts.misconception: ConvNets are not automatically invariant to rotation or scale; the property the book describes is about translation (position shifts).

concepts.name: Spatial hierarchy of patterns
concepts.definition: An organization of visual patterns where larger patterns are built out of smaller ones: edges -> parts -> objects.
concepts.intuition: Letters make words, words make sentences; edges make eyes, eyes and ears make cats.
concepts.technical: Layer l+1 combines local neighbourhoods of layer l feature maps; with downsampling, each unit's receptive field on the original image grows with depth.
concepts.significance: Lets ConvNets efficiently learn increasingly complex and abstract concepts because the visual world is itself hierarchical.
concepts.misconception: The hierarchy is learned, not hand-designed; no one tells layer 2 to detect eyes.

concepts.name: Data efficiency
concepts.definition: Reaching good generalization with fewer training samples.
concepts.intuition: A good prior means fewer examples are needed to learn the rest.
concepts.technical: Architectural priors (locality, weight sharing) restrict the hypothesis space to functions suited to images.
concepts.significance: Explains why ConvNets work even on small image datasets (section 8.2).
concepts.example: A pattern seen in one corner during training need not be seen in all other corners.
concepts.misconception: Data efficiency does not mean ConvNets cannot overfit; on small datasets overfitting remains the main issue (p.291).

deeper.title: Counting what a Dense layer would have to relearn
deeper.body: Beyond the book: a 3 × 3 pattern can be placed at 26 × 26 = 676 positions in a 28 × 28 image (no padding). A Conv2D filter covers all 676 with the **same 9 weights** (plus a bias). A Dense unit that wanted to detect that pattern at every position would effectively need separate weight configurations for each position, and the training data would need to show the pattern at many of them. This is the quantitative face of the book's 'a densely connected model would have to learn the pattern anew'.

deeper.title: Invariance vs equivariance
deeper.body: Note (not in the book): if you shift the input image by a few pixels, a conv layer's response map shifts by the same amount; this is called *equivariance*. The *detection* of the pattern is therefore independent of position, which is what the book means by translation-invariant patterns. Downstream max pooling and global average pooling (p.258) then remove positional information, making the final class prediction approximately invariant.

deeper.title: Hierarchy as a parts list
deeper.body: Think of LEGO: a few basic brick types (edges) combine into subassemblies (windows, wheels, i.e. eyes and ears), which combine into models (a cat). The same brick types appear in many subassemblies, just as in figure 8.2 one line detector feeds several part detectors.

visualizations.title: One 3 × 3 detector, every position
visualizations.why: The page says the MNIST ConvNet looks at 3 × 3 windows and that a learned pattern is recognized anywhere. Step the window over an image with a diagonal stroke (like the digit in figure 8.1) and see the same kernel respond wherever the stroke is.

misconceptions.claim: Convolution layers can only ever see 3 × 3 regions of the image.
misconceptions.correction: Each layer's window is 3 × 3 of its own input, but stacked layers (and pooling) see progressively larger regions of the original image: that is the spatial hierarchy.

misconceptions.claim: Translation invariance means ConvNets also handle rotations and rescaling for free.
misconceptions.correction: The page is about translation: a pattern at a new location. Rotation and scale robustness must be learned (or encouraged with data augmentation, section 8.2.5).

misconceptions.claim: Dense layers cannot recognize a pattern at a new location at all.
misconceptions.correction: They can, but only after learning it anew from examples at that location; this is why they are less data efficient.

takeaways: Dense layers learn global patterns; convolution layers learn local patterns in small 2D windows (3 × 3 in the MNIST model).
ConvNet patterns are translation invariant: learned once, recognized anywhere.
Translation invariance makes ConvNets data efficient, because the visual world is translation invariant.
Stacked conv layers learn spatial hierarchies: edges -> parts -> objects.
Hierarchy lets ConvNets learn increasingly complex and abstract concepts because the visual world is spatially hierarchical.

questions.question: Why does the book say ConvNets are data efficient on images?
options: They have more parameters than dense networks
A pattern learned at one location can be recognized at any other location, so it need not be relearned
questions.answer: A pattern learned at one location can be recognized at any other location, so it need not be relearned
questions.explanation: That is translation invariance, and the book ties data efficiency directly to it. The MNIST ConvNet is not defined by having more parameters, image size is unchanged, and training is still supervised.

questions.question: What size were the windows of the convolution layers in the MNIST example?
questions.explanation: Stated on the page; it corresponds to kernel_size=3 in listing 8.1.

questions.question: Describe in your own words how a second convolution layer can detect a pattern larger than 3 × 3 pixels even though its own kernel is 3 × 3.
questions.answer: Its inputs are the first layer's feature maps, where each position already summarizes a 3 × 3 pixel window; a 3 × 3 window over those maps therefore covers a larger region of the image (5 × 5 without pooling, more with pooling) and combines first-layer features such as edges into larger patterns.
questions.explanation: This is the spatial-hierarchy property: second-layer patterns are made of first-layer features.

questions.question: In figure 8.2, what sits at the middle level of the hierarchy?
options: Simple objects such as eyes or ears
questions.answer: Simple objects such as eyes or ears
questions.explanation: Lines/textures are the lowest learned level, eye/nose/ear the middle, and 'cat' the top. Raw pixels are the input image, not a level of learned modules.

questions.question: The book justifies both properties with a claim about the visual world. What are the two claims, and why does the match between architecture and world matter?
questions.answer: The visual world is fundamentally translation invariant and fundamentally spatially hierarchical. Because ConvNets build in the same structure, they waste no capacity or data learning it, and generalize better from fewer examples.
questions.explanation: Architectural priors that match the data's structure make learning easier; that is the core argument of the page.

questions.question: Could you explain to someone why a dense network on MNIST would need to 'learn the pattern anew' if the same stroke appeared at a new position?
questions.answer: Each pixel has its own weight in a Dense unit, so a stroke at a new position activates different weights that were never trained for it.
questions.explanation: If you can phrase it in terms of separate per-pixel weights vs shared filter weights, you have the key idea.
